lesson.title: Machines that notice
lesson.subtitle: How sensors turn the world into numbers

video.title: Machines that notice
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor, arms full of shopping bags, walks towards a glass supermarket door; it slides open before he reaches it.
scenes.animation: The door slides open; a small question mark pops above it.
scenes.narration: Yesterday I carried two heavy bags to the supermarket door. It slid open before I touched it. Nobody pressed a button. So what noticed me? Let's find out.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: machines that notice, and how they turn the world into numbers.

scenes.visual: A student's face with eyes, ears and nose highlighted; beside it a small circuit board with three tiny sensors.
scenes.animation: Highlights pulse on the face, then on the board's sensors.
scenes.on_screen_text: You have senses; machines have sensors
scenes.narration: You notice the world with your senses. Machines notice it with sensors. A sensor notices just one thing, like light, heat or movement.

scenes.visual: A classroom thermometer; heat waves go in, the number 31 °C comes out.
scenes.animation: Waves flow in; the number counts up to 31.
scenes.on_screen_text: A sensor turns it into a number
scenes.narration: Then the sensor turns what it notices into a number. A thermometer notices heat and says thirty-one degrees. That number is called a reading.

scenes.visual: Four pairs slide in: an eye and a camera, an ear and a microphone, a hand and a thermometer, a nose and a smoke alarm.
scenes.animation: Each pair joins with a click as it is named.
scenes.narration: Many sensors copy one of your senses. A camera sees, like your eyes. A microphone hears, like your ears. A thermometer feels heat, like your skin. And a smoke alarm smells smoke, like your nose.

scenes.visual: A compass needle swinging north; a car reversing with sound arcs from its bumper; a forehead thermometer held a little away from a student's head.
scenes.animation: Each picture pops in as it is named.
scenes.narration: Machines also notice things you can't. A compass feels the Earth's magnetism. A car's parking sensor measures distance with sound too high to hear. A forehead thermometer reads heat without touching.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma beside a drawing of a small kitchen with a charcoal stove and a closed door. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Musa's family cooks on a charcoal stove indoors, with the door shut. Which danger can only a sensor notice?

scenes.visual: An invisible gas shown as a faint dotted cloud; a small alarm on the wall flashes. Then a window opens and a generator sits outside.
scenes.animation: The alarm flashes; the cloud drifts out of the open window.
scenes.narration: A gas with no colour or smell: carbon monoxide. Charcoal or a generator burning in a closed room makes it, and it can kill. Only an alarm can notice it. So run generators outside, and never burn charcoal indoors.

scenes.visual: The supermarket door from the side: a sensor box above it, a tiny chip inside the frame, a motor at the top.
scenes.animation: Each part lights up in turn, joined by arrows.
scenes.narration: Back to the supermarket door. Sense: a motion sensor above it notices something moving close by. Decide: a tiny computer follows its rule, if someone is close, open. Act: a motor slides the door open.

scenes.visual: Three quick panels: a street light at dusk, hands under a dryer, a fridge with a small thermometer inside.
scenes.animation: Panels slide in one by one.
scenes.narration: These three steps are all around you. A street light senses darkness and switches on. A hand dryer senses your hands and blows. A fridge senses it's warming up, and cools again.

scenes.visual: Two columns: a hand switching on a torch and a loudspeaker on one side; a microphone on the other.
scenes.animation: Items drop into each column as they are named.
scenes.narration: Not everything with a switch senses. A torch you switch on senses nothing: you noticed the dark and decided. A microphone takes sound in: it senses. A loudspeaker sends sound out: it acts.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside a school water tank on a stand, a small sensor box on the side and a pump at the bottom. Three answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our school's water tank has a sensor that notices how full it is. When it reads low, the pump starts. Which part decided?

scenes.visual: Three icons line up: a sensor, a number, the sense-decide-act arrows.
scenes.animation: Icons line up right to left in Arabic, left to right in English.
scenes.narration: A small computer, following a rule, decided: the sensor only noticed, and the pump only acted. Remember: a sensor notices one thing and gives a number. Machines sense what you can't. And smart devices sense, decide and act.

scenes.visual: A student with a notebook looks at an automatic tap, a street light and a door; three ticks appear in the notebook.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: go on a sensor hunt at home, at school and on the way. Find things that switch by themselves. For each, write what it senses, what decides and what it does. Next time: your phone's sensors.

checkpoints.prompt: Cooking on charcoal indoors with the door shut: which danger can only a sensor notice?

options.text: A gas with no colour or smell
Smoke drifting up from the stove
Heat building up in the room

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell. You can't notice it, but a carbon monoxide alarm can.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — you can see smoke and feel heat. Carbon monoxide has no colour or smell, so only a sensor can notice it.

checkpoints.prompt: The tank's sensor reads low, and the pump starts. Which part decided to start it?

options.text: The sensor that reads the water level
The pump that pushes the water up
A small computer, following a rule

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the sensor only noticed and the pump only acted. A small computer, following its rule, did the deciding.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a sensor only notices, and a pump only acts. The deciding is done by a small computer following a rule.
